sources.news_title: Hakeem Jeffries Quells Far-Left Revolt to Secure Speaker Nod
sources.text:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries overcame a potential challenge from the party’s progressive wing Wednesday, winning the Democratic nomination for speaker and drawing support from some of his most outspoken critics as he prepares to lead a broad and ideologically varied caucus.
Jeffries prevailed in a secret-ballot vote by 251 to 11, with two members not voting.
Seven members-elect—Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Fredrick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez—voted against him.
The incoming group of progressive lawmakers also pressed Jeffries to embrace a sweeping agenda that includes Medicare for All, tighter restrictions on ICE, campaign finance changes and an end to the war in Gaza. They argued that voters sent them to Washington with a mandate to pursue those priorities.
If he wins the full House vote in January, Jeffries would become the first Black speaker in American history. He would lead Democrats after years in the minority as the party works to turn its election victory into an effective governing majority.
Jeffries had faced criticism from progressives who viewed him as too cautious in challenging President Donald Trump. But he entered Wednesday’s leadership vote without an opponent after making efforts to win over prominent left-wing lawmakers, including New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
The result represented a significant show of support for Jeffries, who has spent months managing frustration within the progressive wing over the Trump administration and demands for a clearer break with the Democratic establishment.
Beyond the House Democratic leadership elections, members were confronted by anti-war protesters who questioned and filmed them.
The campaign against Jeffries moved beyond Capitol Hill as activists promoted an online petition calling on Democrats to reject him and protesters disrupted his appearance at a political conference in Denver the previous week.
Jeffries will lead a large and politically diverse Democratic caucus, including new lawmakers who won districts carried by Trump and may be vulnerable at home or reluctant to support the party on every vote.
Progressives such as California Representative Ro Khanna have urged Jeffries to support tougher positions on issues including ending military aid to Israel, reducing defense spending and advancing Medicare for All.
The effort to block Jeffries had expanded beyond Capitol Hill, with activists promoting an online petition against his leadership and protesters interrupting him during a political conference in Denver the week before.
As Jeffries addressed the crowd, hecklers accused him of failing to stand up for ordinary Americans. The protesters were eventually removed from the event.
The confrontation highlighted the lingering frustration on the left, although supporters in the audience drowned out the demonstrators by chanting Jeffries’ name.
A petition urging Democrats to select someone else had collected more than one million signatures, signaling the depth of activist anger toward party leaders they considered disconnected from the Democratic base.
Still, the online opposition did not produce a congressional challenger, and Jeffries ultimately secured backing from across the caucus.
His victory may mark the start of an even more complicated political balancing act.
Jeffries will oversee a caucus that includes a new wave of lawmakers who won in districts carried by Trump. Many of those members face political risks at home and may not be willing to follow the party line on every vote.
The House majority coalition stretches from progressives representing reliably Democratic districts to moderates who prevailed in areas friendly to Trump.
Jeffries must hold that coalition together while responding to progressives seeking a more forceful agenda and protecting swing-district members from votes that could threaten their reelection prospects.

sources.news_title: Hakeem Jeffries nominated for US House Speaker, set to make history
sources.text:
Hakeem Jeffries set to be first African-American to become US House Speaker
House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker despite limited progressive opposition. The vote moved him closer to becoming the first Black Speaker of the US House.
Democrats have nominated Hakeem Jeffries to lead them in the next US Congress, bringing the New York lawmaker closer to becoming the first Black Speaker of the US House of Representatives.
Jeffries was nominated on Wednesday in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote by the incoming House Democratic Caucus. He secured 251 votes, while 11 Democrats voted against him, reflecting limited internal opposition despite his overwhelming support.
"It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as the Democratic nominee to be the next speaker of the United States House of Representatives," Jeffries said at a press conference.
Addressing the opposition, Jeffries said Democrats should focus on fighting "MAGA extremism" rather than engaging in internal divisions, adding that the party must work together to "get big things done for the American people."
The nomination comes amid demands from some incoming progressive lawmakers for stronger commitments to a more ambitious policy agenda, including populist measures they campaigned on during the November 3 midterm elections.
A group of seven incoming progressives said in a joint statement that they voted against Jeffries because they were still seeking assurances from the New York Democrat on the party's direction in the next Congress.
"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership," they said, adding that discussions were ongoing.
DEMOCRATS PLAY DOWN INTERNAL DIFFERENCES
Leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus congratulated Jeffries and pledged to work with him on measures including Medicare for All and ending for-profit immigrant detention centres.
Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the progressive group who voted for Jeffries, said incoming lawmakers were justified in wanting to respond to public anger and believed Jeffries understood those demands.
Other Democratic lawmakers also played down the opposition, arguing that disagreements were part of the political process and would not undermine the party's leadership.
Representative Emanuel Cleaver told Reuters that opposition was inevitable, while Representative Jonathan Jackson said Democrats could have a majority without needing complete agreement among members.
Despite the dissent, Jeffries is widely expected to be elected Speaker when the new Congress convenes in early January. The position requires 218 votes on the House floor and places its holder second in line to the US presidency.
Democrats are expected to hold at least 257 seats in the House, although several competitive races remain uncalled.
HISTORIC MILESTONE FOR DEMOCRATS
Jeffries' nomination was also celebrated as a historic moment for the party.
Representative Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, who was the highest-ranking Black Democrat in the House before Jeffries became the party's leader, described Wednesday's vote as "very historic".
Representative Joe Morelle, a fellow New York Democrat who has known Jeffries for nearly two decades, expressed confidence in his leadership, saying he would make a great Speaker.
Representative Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania also welcomed the party's electoral gains, describing the nomination as part of a broader turnaround following Election Day.
Meanwhile, House Republicans last week nominated Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to lead their conference in January. Jordan defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise after outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not seek to lead Republicans in the minority.

sources.news_title: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to become first Black US Speaker - The Tribune
sources.text:
Washington DC [US], November 19 (ANI): House Democrats have nominated Hakeem Jeffries to lead the party in the new Congress, putting him on course to become the first Black Speaker of the US House of Representatives when the chamber convenes in January.
Democrats voted to back Jeffries for the top leadership position roughly two weeks after their midterm election victory, despite opposition from a small group of newly elected lawmakers on the party's far-left who had demanded policy commitments in exchange for their support.
Only 11 Democrats voted against Jeffries in the secret ballot, according to a source familiar with the vote, effectively clearing the way for him to secure the speakership. A formal vote by the full House on January 3, the first day of the new Congress, remains the final step before he can assume the position. Even his detractors are expected to support his election, CNN reported.
Speaking to reporters after securing the nomination, Jeffries said that Americans were seeking substantial changes and that Democrats were committed to addressing their expectations.
"People of this country are demanding big, dramatic and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable. And we're committed to delivering in a meaningful way the type of change that the American people deserve," he said.
However, a group of seven newly elected progressive Democrats said they voted against Jeffries because they were seeking commitments on key policy priorities, including holding votes on Medicare for All and ending what they described as "the genocide in Gaza."
The statement was signed by Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez of Pennsylvania and New York, respectively.
Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard also told CNN that he voted against Jeffries' nomination, saying he wanted assurances that the incoming leadership would prioritise campaign finance reform and efforts to block US aid to Israel.
"We're looking for a strong commitment to end the Citizens United this Congress through a 28th Amendment, and we're looking, looking to call a vote on US aid to Israel. Until I get confirmation on those votes, he does not have my support. We've got until the first week of January; I'm still holding out hope," Leonard said as quoted by CNN as saying.
Responding to the opposition within the party, Jeffries said, "Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other."
Ahead of the leadership vote, Jeffries received a strong endorsement from Representative Jim Clyburn, a longtime ally and one of the most senior members of the Congressional Black Caucus. Clyburn addressed the caucus as it formally nominated Jeffries, delivering a speech that two people present in the room described as powerful, according to CNN.
"Hakeem is interested in headways and not headlines," Clyburn said in his remarks.
Jeffries had been widely expected to secure the nomination, given the Democrats' sizeable majority in the upcoming Congress, which would make it difficult for a small group of lawmakers to influence the leadership election.
Nevertheless, the New York Democrat did not take the outcome for granted. Ahead of the vote, he held face-to-face discussions with incoming Democratic lawmakers who had not publicly committed to supporting him, most of whom were aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America.
He also met different factions within the party, including centrists, the New Democrat Coalition, the Blue Dog Caucus and the Congressional Progressive Caucus. His team, however, kept the details of the private discussions closely guarded.
Earlier on Friday, Jeffries announced his support for major elements of a universal healthcare system, including lowering the eligibility age for Medicare, establishing a new programme guaranteeing universal coverage for children and expanding Medicare coverage to include hearing, dental and vision care.
Meanwhile, Jeffries' leadership team is expected to include Representative Katherine Clark as House majority leader, making her the first woman to hold the position, and Representative Pete Aguilar as whip, who would become the first Latino to occupy the chamber's third-highest leadership position.
Jeffries' appointment comes after Democrats registered gains in the midterm elections, with the party projected to take control of both chambers of Congress. (ANI)
(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

sources.news_title: ‘I had tremendous leverage’: Pressley explains how she navigated speaker interest — and ultimately supported Jeffries - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday was overwhelmingly chosen by House Democrats to be their nominee for speaker for next Congress, tamping down an intense burst of activist interest in having Boston Representative Ayanna Pressley be speaker, instead.
Pressley did not openly embrace the idea as it gained momentum online, but she also did not explicitly reject it.
In the end, Pressley told the Globe in an interview, she voted yes to support Jeffries’s speakership, along with 250 other Democrats. But, she revealed, in the days preceding the vote, she did leave open the possibility of allowing a colleague to nominate her for the role, and engaged in an intense sprint of negotiations to pressure the incoming House leadership team on the progressive agenda she has championed.
“I had clarity that I was not going to mount a bid for the speakership,” Pressley said, emphasizing her focus was on policy and not herself. “However, I was also very clear that I had tremendous leverage, and I was not going to cede that ground until after many, many, many, many hours of negotiations.”
Jeffries easily won the nomination for speaker in a closed-door meeting of returning and incoming House Democrats on Wednesday, securing 251 yes votes to 11 no votes — well above the 218 that will be necessary on the House floor on Jan. 3. There was no challenger. In a news conference after the vote, Jeffries pledged to use the majority to enact a sweeping agenda.
“The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic, and transformational change,” Jeffries said. “And we’re committed to delivering, in a meaningful way, the type of change that the American people deserve.”
Pressley said “bold” is exactly what she pushed for in hours of talks. She sought to ensure that Democrats would not water down policy in order to avoid a veto from President Trump and move on top priority items, including abortion and reproductive rights and what she calls a reparative justice agenda for Black Americans. She said she did not receive specific commitments on legislation, but rather emerged from the talks with a confidence that Jeffries would act with urgency and would not sideline progressives to protect battleground moderates.
“After intense negotiations ... I had a confidence in his ability to be moved,” Pressley said. “The people who call this country home cannot afford for us to only advance an agenda that we believe is veto-proof — that is failure. Because the people who call this country home are very smart; they know we’re not going to win every fight, but they want to see us do it.”
Jeffries’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It’s not clear how much support Pressley ever had inside the House for the job. She and her office said she received an outpouring of support from colleagues, but wouldn’t reveal hard numbers.
Pressley had already spent months in discussion with leadership and other progressives as well as with groups like the Congressional Black Caucus and outside advocacy organizations. She has also met with incoming new staunch progressive and democratic socialist members who were eager to use their growing numbers to push for their priorities in a new Democratic majority.
In a conversation with the Globe in October, Pressley had called Jeffries and the other top leaders, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark of Revere and California Representative Pete Aguilar, “thoughtful partners” and gave no indication she would challenge them.
At the time, progressives had anticipated they might have serious leverage in a narrow House majority. But after the election resulted in a massive blue wave that gave Democrats at least 257 seats, progressives’ negotiating power became diminished. Still, Jeffries never expressed any doubt that in the days after the election he had the votes to become speaker.
Then in early November, an online petition for Pressley to be speaker began circulating and has reached more than 150,000 signatures. It was started by a group calling itself the Coalition for Speaker Ayanna Pressley, which also launched a website, and the idea began to pick up steam among outside activists as callers flooded congressional phone lines with demands to not support Jeffries for speaker.
Pressley said in her office on Wednesday that the groundswell was “organic” and not affiliated with her, but when she saw the momentum behind it, she recognized it was an opportunity to intensify the conversations with leadership. To the anonymous grumbling of some colleagues, Pressley did not explicitly tamp down the speakership talk, calling herself “humbled” by the calls and discussing her preferred policies.
“I wasn’t playing coy,” Pressley said. “Everybody here has tools, and everybody here has power. You get to decide how to steward your power, and you get to decide how to utilize your leverage. This was my leverage to advance our shared priorities.”
Pressley noted her years of experience in Congress, on Boston City Council, and as a congressional staffer in the Capitol when it came to recognizing a moment to put some progressive pressure on Jeffries.
She also said that despite backing Jeffries, she expects there will still be times when there will be disagreement within the caucus, and that’s part of the process of governing.
“I agitate and push and organize and exhaust, no matter who has the gavel,” Pressley said. “So, in many ways, it matters to me who it is, and in many ways, it doesn’t, because it doesn’t change how I move. I’m still going to demand, push, and organize for more.”

sources.news_title: Jeffries Nominated by Fellow Democrats to Be House Speaker, Vows 'To Hold the Crooks Accountable'
sources.text:
by Kevin Killough
House Democrats on Wednesday picked fellow party member Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as their nominee for House speaker in the new Congress next year.
“We’re going to fight in the face of the unprecedented corruption, chaos and cruelty visited upon the American people, that House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable,” Jeffries said in accepting the nomination.
He also said House Democrats were committed to helping people who are “drowning in this failed Republican economy.”
Jeffries, of New York, won 251-11, amid only slight opposition from progressives seeking a shift in the party’s direction,
As speaker, Jeffries will be the chamber’s top lawmaker, following his party on Nov. 3 winning the House and Senate majority.
Jeffries also signaled that Democrats plan to make good on threats to launch investigations against President Donald Trump, his family and his aides.
He must now win the full House vote in January before the position becomes final. With Democrats expected to hold more than 250 seats next year, Jeffries is likely to get the 218 votes needed to secure his position.
The caucus also voted to make Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts the next majority leader.
California Democratic Rep. Mike Levin said on social media that he was “proud to stand with 250 of my colleagues as he won our caucus nomination overwhelmingly.”
“Hakeem is a good friend and has been a steady hand through some of the most turbulent years this institution has seen. He kept our big, diverse caucus together, listened to every corner of it, and led us to our largest House majority in more than three decades. From Brooklyn to the Speaker’s chair, his story shows what this country can be,” Levin said.
“When the full House votes in January, he will become the first African American Speaker in our nation’s history. I can’t wait to get to work with him on lowering costs and holding power accountable for every family we serve,” he added.
New Mexico Democratic Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández said, “John Adams said the House should be ‘an exact portrait of the American people at large.’ Speaker Jeffries led the election of 262 Democrats who will serve in the People’s House next year, making sure that the portrait of our Congress looks like the beautiful mosaic that is America.”
– – –
Kevin Killough is a reporter for Just the News. Zachery Schmidt is the digital editor of The Star News Network and contributed to this story.

sources.news_title: Jeffries set to be first black speaker of US House
sources.text:
Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of becoming the first black speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats elected him their leader on Wednesday following a sweeping midterm election triumph.
The 56-year-old New Yorker secured 251 votes in a closed-door, secret ballot, with 11 cast against his nomination, according to US media.
Jeffries faced no declared challenger, although opposition from some newly elected progressives had exposed divisions over how Democrats should wield their newfound power.
His nomination puts him on course to preside over a commanding Democratic majority during the final two years of US President Donald Trump's term, as his party prepares to reverse Republican policies and investigate the administration.
Jeffries must still win a formal vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes on January 3, when he would become the first black politician to hold the powerful post. With a large Democratic majority, this is seen as something of a formality.
Both returning Democrats and incoming lawmakers participated in Wednesday's election, including progressives who had sought concessions on issues ranging from US military support for Israel to the influence of money in politics.
Jeffries had requested a recorded vote rather than a nomination "by acclamation" – without a formal ballot – as some allies had hoped.
He argued that every Democrat should have an opportunity to weigh his experience, record and vision, citing the precedent set when the party last took control of the House in 2018.
The ballot remained secret, with the overall tally made public but individual votes kept anonymous.
Ahead of the election, Jeffries met progressive lawmakers to discuss issues including Israel and healthcare, with proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage among the topics discussed.
The Democratic leader has also sought to shift attention to the party's plans for governing after voters handed Republicans a crushing defeat amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel costs.
"Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one," he told reporters on Tuesday.
"We're going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America."
Raised in Brooklyn's working-class Crown Heights neighborhood, Jeffries trained as a lawyer before entering the New York state legislature in 2007 and winning election to Congress in 2012.
Known for his measured manner, sharp rhetoric and penchant for quoting hip-hop artists, he became the first black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress when Democrats chose him to succeed Nancy Pelosi in 2022.
He also served as a House prosecutor during Trump's first impeachment trial in 2020.
As speaker, Jeffries would preside over one of Washington's most powerful institutions and stand second in line to the presidency behind the vice president.
But he would face a formidable task in managing a Democratic coalition spanning centrists and an increasingly assertive left flank.
His party has promised investigations into Trump and his administration, while lawmakers remain divided over Israel, healthcare and how aggressively to pursue their agenda against a president who retains veto power.
Jeffries's nomination contrasts with a more competitive leadership contest among Senate Democrats, where veteran party chief Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from progressive Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen.
Van Hollen has attracted support from prominent left-wing figures, including Bernie Sanders, but acknowledges he is the underdog. Senate Democrats will elect their leader in early December.
Republicans chose their own congressional leaders last week, elevating Trump ally Jim Jordan in the House and retaining John Thune in the Senate. (AFP)

Brooklyn’s Hakeem Jeffries wins historic speaker nomination, but two incoming NYC House members vote against him
sources.text:
Brooklyn Rep. Hakeem Jeffries secured the Democratic nomination for House speaker on Wednesday, moving one step closer to becoming the first Black person to hold the position in American history, despite opposition from two incoming members of New York City’s congressional delegation.
Jeffries, 56, ran unopposed and won the closed-door House Democratic Caucus election 251-11, according to several media outlets. He faces a formal vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3.
If elected in January, Jeffries would also become the first New Yorker to serve as House speaker since 1869, when Republican Theodore M. Pomeroy held the position for a single day — the shortest speakership in American history.
Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, both democratic socialists who received Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s endorsement during their congressional campaigns, were among seven incoming Democrats who publicly confirmed they voted against Jeffries.
In a joint statement following Wednesday’s vote, the lawmakers said they had been in discussions with Jeffries about securing commitments on several of their policy priorities.
“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the lawmakers said. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”
The statement was also signed by incoming Reps. Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania.
“While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they said. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”
Valdez was elected earlier this month to represent New York’s 7th Congressional District, which covers parts of Brooklyn and Queens, while Avila Chevalier will represent the 13th Congressional District, spanning Upper Manhattan and the Bronx. Neither indicated in the statement how they intend to vote in January.
At a press conference in Washington on Wednesday, Jeffries stressed the need for party unity when asked about divisions within the Democratic caucus.
“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries said.

Since the House first convened in 1789, no Black American has held the speaker’s gavel. Jeffries’ expected election on January 3, 2027, would break that barrier after 237 years.
Among those nominating him was veteran South Carolina congressman Jim Clyburn, a former House majority whip, civil rights veteran and longtime political mentor.
“This is a very surreal moment for me,” Clyburn told reporters.
Jeffries, a Brooklyn native and former attorney, became the first Black lawmaker to lead either major party in Congress when Democrats elevated him to their leadership position in 2022.
As speaker, he would stand second in the presidential line of succession, behind the vice president, while wielding substantial influence over legislation, committee leadership and federal spending.
That authority could prove especially consequential for Black communities on issues ranging from voting rights and economic opportunity to health care, education and federal civil rights protections. However, the extent of his influence would depend on negotiations with the Senate and White House.
Progressive Democrats Signal They Want More
Although Jeffries won overwhelmingly, 11 Democrats voted against his nomination, exposing disagreements over the party’s direction.
Seven dissenting lawmakers, including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Frederick Haynes of Texas and Claire Valdez of New York, issued a joint statement explaining their opposition.
“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote.
The lawmakers acknowledged progress in discussions with Jeffries but said additional commitments were necessary.
“Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” they concluded.
With Democrats projected to hold 259 House seats, Jeffries enters the January 3 floor vote with a substantial numerical advantage, although he must still secure a majority of votes cast for a named candidate.
New Leadership, New Expectations
Jeffries will lead a Democratic leadership team reflecting several historic breakthroughs.
Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts was elected majority leader, becoming the first woman to hold that position in either chamber. California Rep. Pete Aguilar will serve as majority whip, while Rep. Ted Lieu becomes the first Asian American Democratic Caucus chairman. Colorado Rep. Joe Neguse was elected assistant speaker.
Jeffries has already begun meeting with progressive and moderate Democratic factions to establish priorities for the incoming Congress, including affordability and economic concerns.
“It’s a great class, and they have a lot of wonderful ideas, fresh ideas, new ideas about how to advance the ball in a bold way for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters.
For Clyburn, whose political career was shaped by the Civil Rights Movement, the moment represents another chapter in a decades-long struggle for Black representation at the highest levels of American government.
For Jeffries, the challenge ahead is turning that historic breakthrough into legislative results.

sources.news_title: Hakeem Jeffries gets party nod as House Speaker, but NYC's left remains wary
sources.text:
U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries moved a step closer to becoming speaker of the House of Representatives Wednesday, even as two democratic socialists in New York City’s congressional delegation voted against him.
House Democrats backed Jeffries 251-11 in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote, multiple news outlets reported. Jeffries, who ran unopposed, will have to wait until the full House votes to officially claim the gavel, but there’s little doubt now that he’ll become the country’s first Black speaker.
Reps.-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, two members of the Democratic Socialists of America, released a statement with five other members-elect from outside New York explaining their decision to vote against Jeffries’ nomination.
“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the group said. “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”
Jeffries, who represents New York's 8th Congressional District in Central Brooklyn, is seen as a centrist who has been reluctant to embrace some of the DSA’s platform, most notably its criticism of Israel. Jeffries waited for months to endorse Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral run last year, even as he faced off against former Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Republican Curtis Sliwa.
Wednesday’s nomination comes after months of pushback from Jeffries’ left, much of it from his own city. In June’s primaries, Avila Chevalier unseated Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom Jeffries had endorsed. At Valdez’s primary-night party, her supporters chanted “You’re next!” when Jeffries appeared on a TV screen. Earlier, City Councilmember Chi Ossé, a DSA member, had briefly moved to challenge Jeffries himself but backed off.
Ultimately, Jeffries won the nomination easily. No challenger came forward, and two of the city’s most prominent progressives, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, stood by him.
When asked by reporters about the democratic socialists’ comments, Jeffries said he was looking forward to working with all members of his party.
“It’s an honor to be serving with a majority of 260 members from all across the country,” he said. “People who have different perspectives, and we embrace that, but we’re gonna work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people.”
Grace Mauser, co-chair of the city’s chapter of the DSA, applauded the members who resisted supporting Jeffries.
“I am hopeful that the 'no' votes he’s seeing, in conjunction with the thousands of calls his members are getting, remind him that his constituency is not just the Democratic House members, it’s actually all of Americans,” she said. “American voters were very clear earlier this month. They were clear that they want a leader of the Democratic Party with a real backbone.”
She said Jeffries needs to make real progress on issues like Medicare for All, universal childcare and ending the war in Iran.
“If he doesn’t take that seriously, I don’t think he’s equipped to be leader in this moment,” she said.
Brigid Bergin contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: Hakeem Jeffries Wins Democrats’ Speaker Nomination Ahead of House Vote - FINCHANNEL
sources.text:
Hakeem Jeffries won the Democratic nomination for House speaker Wednesday, securing 251 of 262 ballots in a closed-door vote and advancing toward a separate election by the full chamber in January. If elected, the New York Democrat would become the first Black speaker in the country’s history.
The result, reported by The Associated Press and independently corroborated by CBS, gave Jeffries his party’s backing as Democrats prepared to take the majority. He ran unopposed. The nomination did not itself install him as speaker.
The New York Post reported that the caucus voted 251 to 11, using a yes-or-no ballot. Jeffries had sought a counted vote instead of nomination by acclamation, allowing colleagues to record opposition even without an alternative candidate.
The Post noted that he had pointed to the approach Democrats used in 2018, when Nancy Pelosi won the party’s nomination with 203 supporters and more than 30 opponents. Wednesday’s vote was an internal party decision; members will vote again in the public House election.
Policy demands preceded the ballot
Before the vote, Reuters reported differing views among incoming Democrats. Adam Hamawy of New Jersey wanted a discussion of policy plans before committing his support. William Lawrence of Michigan said he intended to honor an earlier promise to back Jeffries while seeking a more ambitious agenda.
Incoming members Melat Kiros of Colorado and Claire Valdez of New York emphasized the party’s program rather than the identity of its leader, Reuters reported. Those public comments preceded the private ballot and do not establish how any of them voted Wednesday.
Jeffries has led Democrats in the minority since 2023, Reuters reported.
What the floor election requires
The full House election is expected January 3, when the new Congress convenes. Its voting rules differ from a party nomination contest. Under the procedure described by the Congressional Research Service, the winner needs a majority of votes cast for a named person, with a quorum present.
That requirement often produces a threshold of 218 in a fully participating, 435-member House. It can be lower if members are absent or answer present, because a present response does not count as a vote for a named candidate.
The CRS explanation, updated April 21, says members may vote for someone other than the major parties’ nominees. If nobody receives the required majority, another ballot follows. Candidates are not eliminated simply for receiving fewer votes on an earlier ballot.
Members state their choice aloud during the roll call, a practice used since 1839. These procedures leave the January result to the members participating in that election, regardless of the outcome of Wednesday’s nomination.
A different role from party leader
The House clerk’s description of congressional leadership separates the speaker’s election by the whole membership from other leadership choices made within party delegations. It identifies the Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference as the formal organizations through which each party conducts its internal affairs.
As the current Democratic minority leader, Jeffries directs his party’s legislative strategy and serves as a principal spokesperson. The speaker, by contrast, presides over the House and acts as its administrative head, as well as leading the majority party.
Other leadership posts divide responsibilities for legislation and party coordination. The majority leader helps plan the agenda and schedule business. Whips communicate between leaders and members, assemble support for priorities and mobilize votes on legislation.
Those responsibilities extend beyond the nomination contest. The clerk describes House leadership as chosen every two years at the beginning of a Congress, with the full chamber and the party delegations exercising different roles in the selection process.
The agenda Jeffries put before colleagues
Jeffries announced his candidacy in a November 4 letter asking colleagues to support him for speaker. He organized his proposed agenda around affordability, accountability and American values, while promising that members across the majority would have a role in developing it.
The letter identified five policy areas already assigned to Democratic working groups: housing, health care, groceries and goods, gas and utilities, and caregiving. Jeffries said Democrats would seek bipartisan agreements where possible while pressing to reduce household costs.
His proposals included reversing Medicaid reductions, restoring nutrition assistance funding, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits and changing tariff policy. He also called for a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and for greater oversight of the executive branch.
These were the candidate’s stated priorities for the coming Congress. The letter did not establish that the proposals had passed either chamber, received presidential approval or secured the support of every incoming Democrat. Wednesday’s leadership vote likewise was not a vote on a legislative package.
Under the letter’s American values heading, Jeffries emphasized equal protection, voting rights and the country’s immigrant heritage. He said he wanted to draw on perspectives from every part of the caucus.
Legislation requires more than a House majority
The House’s explanation of the legislative process describes committee consideration, debate and voting as stages through which a bill can advance. A proposal approved by the House must also pass the Senate. Differences between the chambers’ versions have to be resolved before legislation can be presented to the president.
The president can sign a bill or veto it. A measure may also become law without his signature under the constitutional process. A House speaker’s authority over the chamber’s business therefore operates within a process that also includes senators and the executive branch; the party nomination does not itself confer the power to enact Jeffries’s proposed agenda.
A Brooklyn lawmaker’s route to leadership
Jeffries represents New York’s Eighth Congressional District and is serving his seventh House term. His congressional biography records unanimous elections as Democratic leader in 2022 and 2024. He previously chaired the Democratic Caucus and served as whip of the Congressional Black Caucus.
Before entering Congress, he spent six years in the New York State Assembly. His biography describes work on policing records, affordable housing and the civil court system. He was born in Brooklyn, raised in Crown Heights and attended Midwood High School.
He earned a political science degree from the State University of New York at Binghamton, a master’s degree in public policy from Georgetown University and a law degree from New York University. His legal career included a clerkship for federal Judge Harold Baer Jr. in Manhattan.
He subsequently practiced at Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison and worked as litigation counsel for Viacom and CBS, according to his official biography. His progression through state government, Congress and party leadership preceded his bid to become the House’s presiding officer.
The office at stake
The House historian traces the speakership to Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution, which gives the chamber the power to choose its speaker and other officers. Frederick Augustus Conrad Muhlenberg of Pennsylvania became the first speaker on April 1, 1789.
The office developed beyond its early role as a presiding and ceremonial position. The historian describes the modern speaker as both a political and parliamentary leader, with the House and individual officeholders shaping the position’s responsibilities over time.
The House’s historical record counts 56 people who have held the office through Mike Johnson. Several served nonconsecutive periods, including Henry Clay, Sam Rayburn and Nancy Pelosi. The speaker is also second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president.
FAQ
Is Jeffries already speaker?
No. Democrats nominated him Wednesday. The full House election is expected when the new Congress convenes January 3.
Does a speaker always need 218 votes?
No. The requirement is a majority of votes cast for a named person, so attendance and present votes can change the threshold.

sources.news_title: Hakeem Jeffries Nominated, Could Be First Black House Speaker
sources.text:
Hakeem Jeffries Wins Democratic Nomination, Moves One Step From Becoming First Black Speaker
House Democrats nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker in a closed-door caucus vote Nov. 18, giving him 251 of 262 ballots ahead of the full House vote on Jan. 3. If elected, Jeffries would be the first Black speaker in the chamber’s history. A progressive campaign has argued he is too cautious, and seven representatives-elect say they voted no. Emory political scientist Andra Gillespie says no serious challenger has emerged and some members want to vote for the first Black speaker. Progressive leaders including Greg Casar and Pramila Jayapal say they plan to push Jeffries toward a bold agenda.
House Democrats on Nov. 18 nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as their candidate for speaker, moving the Brooklyn, New York, congressman one step from becoming the first Black person to hold one of Washington’s most powerful offices.
Jeffries won 251 of 262 ballots cast in a closed-door caucus vote, well above the 218 votes he will need when the full House elects a speaker on Jan. 3. No one challenged him for the nomination, and he asked for a tallied vote rather than winning by acclamation.
The vote capped a remarkable two weeks. When the blue tsunami surged across the country on Election Day, it delivered Democrats a commanding majority in Congress and swept Jeffries to the edge of history. It is a moment generations in the making, unimaginable even during Reconstruction, when Southern voters sent newly emancipated Americans to Congress.
But the path to the gavel has not been entirely smooth. Even as Jeffries prepares to join the ranks of era-defining speakers such as Nancy Pelosi, Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill and Newt Gingrich, a progressive groundswell has built against him. Activists convinced that voters gave Democrats a mandate for wholesale change argued that Jeffries is too cautious, too closely aligned with the party establishment and too willing to negotiate with President Donald Trump and MAGA Republicans. They flooded congressional offices with phone calls, an online petition gathered more than a million signatures and social media filled with demands that Democrats choose someone else.
That pressure showed up in the caucus vote. Seven representatives-elect, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez, released a joint statement afterward saying they had voted no. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” the statement said.
Before the vote, Kiros told The Lever that she wanted a leader who would prioritize progressive goals such as Medicare for all and stronger regulation of Big Tech. “If that’s not a priority of yours, then I don’t think you should be speaker,” she said.
The irony is hard to ignore. At the very moment Black political power is poised to reach a new level, some of the loudest voices trying to stop it come from the progressive left, a movement that has long championed racial justice and equality.
Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at Emory University, said the dissatisfaction with Jeffries is real. But several factors, including Jeffries’ race, internal party politics and the “thankless” nature of the job, kept would-be contenders on the sidelines.
“There are people who are complaining. There are people who are saying they won’t support Jeffries,” Gillespie said. “But nobody seems to be stepping up to want to give him a serious challenge.”
At the same time, she said, “There are people who have openly said, ‘I want to vote for the first Black speaker of the House.’”
Among members, “I think that there is a certain reticence to scuttling the nomination of the first Black speaker of the House,” Gillespie said. She noted that even an influential potential challenger like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York might struggle to gather enough votes, assuming she wanted the job.
Not every progressive joined the revolt. Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, emphasized working with Jeffries rather than replacing him. “We’re not a caucus of breaking things. We’re a caucus of ‘yes,’ and of building things,” Casar told Bloomberg, according to The Lever. Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington, a former caucus chair, said progressives intend to push Jeffries toward an ambitious agenda. “We will be driving an agenda that truly is big and bold,” she told Axios.
Jeffries’ supporters dismissed the opposition. Rep. Sam Liccardo of California told Axios that Jeffries has his support, “and anybody talking about a challenger is just selling tickets to a circus with no tent.” Rep. Marc Veasey of Texas described the Democratic victory as a triumph of “common sense, not any extremist ideology.”
The final test comes Jan. 3. The caucus vote was a secret ballot, but on the House floor, each member must stand and announce their choice on live television. That could be difficult for progressives who have been flooded with calls urging them to vote against Jeffries. A handful of incoming members, including Reps.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres of California and Don Leonard of Ohio, have said outright that they will oppose him.
Gillespie said Jeffries should not dismiss his critics. “It suggests he is going to have to be responsive to some of the interests of progressive members of the House,” she said. “He’s at least got to make an effort to show that he is being sensitive to their needs and being as responsive as he possibly can be.”
Jeffries has not ignored the warning signs. In his Nov. 4 letter announcing his candidacy, he pledged to pursue three priorities: “Affordability,” “Accountability” and “American Values.” Asked recently whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should be impeached, Jeffries answered, “Hard yes.”
His race carries particular weight for a party whose 2026 dominance was powered by Black voters. Black women backed Democrats at 92%, and 8 in 10 Black men voted for the party. By contrast, about half of white women and 47% of white men voted Democratic. The push for a progressive alternative may be legitimate, but it risks alienating the voters who carried Democrats to power.
Jeffries’ rise would also mark a milestone in a Congress that long excluded Black Americans. In 1870, Joseph H. Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House. More than 150 years later, no Black lawmaker has held its highest office.
Pelosi handpicked Jeffries to succeed her as Democratic leader after the 2022 midterms, and he was elected unopposed. Since then, he has held his caucus together through the party’s years in the minority and helped engineer its sweeping 2026 victory.
For Jeffries, the challenge now is holding together a party whose victory has exposed competing ideas about what to do with power. For progressives, the question is how to square a commitment to expanding Black political representation with opposition to the first Black lawmaker poised to lead the House.
For Democrats, the answer could shape far more than who holds the gavel.
This article first appeared in Word In Black. It has been edited for style and updated with the results of the Nov. 18 House Democratic caucus vote. Read the original at wordinblack.com.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP)—Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker with the gavel.
Jeffries secured the nod during closed-door voting, with 251 of the 262 ballots cast, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.
He ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media posts have been flooding the offices of Democrats and the newly elected, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.
Ahead of Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries, of New York, said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members in what will be their large majority.
“I embrace those conversations,” he said.
Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts—Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.
Jeffries will face a separate roll call of the whole House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.
Skeptics Question Whether Leaders Are Up to the Job
Wednesday’s vote was the first of their careers for dozens of members-elect, before they’re even sworn into office in January. With one of the biggest incoming majorities in decades, Jeffries will have room to spare.
Rep.-elect Brad Lander of New York announced he would support Jeffries when he launched his campaign for Congress. Rep.-elect Randy Villegas of California has said he was supporting whoever would help him best deliver for his Central Valley district.
Returning Rep. Emily Randall of Washington said she heard questions about House leadership during town halls in her district and had been watching direct messages stream into her Instagram feed about the leadership election. So she decided to start dialing them back.
“People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the House,” she said, referring to the Vermont independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. “Technically yes, and it would be probably difficult.”
(It’s true that the House can elect anyone speaker, but it’s unlikely to be Sanders because he already has his day job in the Senate.)
On one call, Randall said, she listened to the constituent’s concerns and then replied, “Truthfully, not like blowing smoke, whoever is our speaker—and I think it is going to be Hakeem Jeffries, and I am supporting Hakeem Jeffries for speaker—I think we will accomplish a lot of the things that he was asking us to.”
Lawmakers pointed to the livestream that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York did trying to explain the role of the speaker.
“There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the Capitol. “I think that everyone is far more concerned what that leadership means, what is it promising.”
First Leaders of a Post-Pelosi Era
Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders of the post-Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.
When Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California decided to step aside from leadership in 2022 after the party’s electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era. Pelosi, No. 2 Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina had often moved together, rising, and then stepping back, from their long-held positions.
A similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.
Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House “are quite different.”
She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others. “His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction,” Ansari said.
“It is more productive to focus on preparing on what we’re going to do in the majority and what we need and want to get done in those first 100 days,” she said.
Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who pulled off a stunning victory in a redrawn district favoring the Republican candidate, said before the vote that he’d be supporting Jeffries.
“It’s not even like a complex question,” he said about Jeffries, who he said “led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation.”
“I’m not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history,” he said.

sources.news_title: CT Dems align behind Hakeem Jeffries' bid to be House speaker
sources.text:
Connecticut’s congressional delegation on Wednesday rallied behind Hakeem Jeffries’ bid to serve as speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives when Democrats assume control next year with one of the largest majorities in decades.
House Democrats’ internal leadership election is the first step in the process for the New York Democrat, but it puts him on track to become the first Black speaker when the entire House votes on Jan. 3 in the incoming session of Congress.
Jeffries has sought to shore up support across an ideologically diverse caucus that includes moderates representing the reddest parts of the country to progressives in liberal enclaves. With a 251-11 vote on Wednesday, Democrats hope any tension over his nomination is resolved.
The leadership elections happened behind closed doors, and the Democratic caucus — which included newly elected members of Congress — voted in secret. Aside from nominations for speaker, the party is also voting on nominations for other leadership roles, like caucus chair.
While Democrats saw massive wins in the midterm elections earlier this month, some voters argue that it’s an indication that they want to see new leadership in both the House and Senate. Local grassroots groups in Connecticut and elsewhere wanted lawmakers to support alternatives to Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, who is running to become Senate majority leader next year, a post he once held.
No formal challenger materialized against Jeffries for Speaker of the House. The Senate, meanwhile, has a contested race for majority leader that also features U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Schumer claimed Wednesday he has the votes to overcome that challenge in leadership elections that are slated for early December. (U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said he supports Schumer for the role.)
In the lead-up to these leadership elections, groups like Connecticut 50501 encouraged people to make daily calls to the offices of their elected officials to support candidacies other than Jeffries and Schumer.
Even with opposition percolating, U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, had predicted for weeks that Jeffries would have no issue getting the speaker nomination. Jeffries has been serving as House minority leader since 2023 and is a close ally of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California.
“I’ve had any number of conversations with people. I get the concern,” Himes said last week on Connecticut Public’s “The Wheelhouse.” “Hakeem is an unknown quantity. He’s stepping into Nancy Pelosi’s shoes, and she was the ultimate in known quantities.”
“My own view is that Hakeem deserves a chance,” he continued. “I also don’t want to necessarily run over or see run over the absolutely historic moment of an African American man serving as speaker of the House for the first time in 250 years.”
Himes is expected to take the helm of the House Intelligence Committee next year. As speaker, Jeffries would appoint Democrats to the committee.
U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Bronin confirmed during new member orientation that he’d support Jeffries for speaker. Bronin defeated U.S. Rep. John Larson in the Democratic primary for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District.
Jeffries supported Larson’s reelection bid and came to Hartford to campaign with the longtime congressman before Connecticut’s summer primary. At the time, Bronin said leadership should spend “less time protecting people who’ve been in Congress for decades and more time working to lift up a new generation of Democrats to help us build a stronger, more energetic, more effective Democratic Party.”
In an interview a day before the speaker vote, Bronin said Jeffries has never gotten the chance to wield the gavel and lead from the majority party.
“He’s kept a Democratic caucus together in very difficult times, and he has stayed laser-focused on the twin missions of affordability for working families and accountability for a president who’s out of control,” Bronin said Tuesday. “And after two terms in the minority, without the votes to make make change, I think he’s earned the chance to lead a majority to make the change we need.”
That’s something U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, echoed as someone who’s been in the minority party for the past four years.
Courtney, who was first elected in 2006, said he’s served in the minority party in previous sessions and has seen more progress and even some victories this time around. He pointed to the number of discharge petitions, a procedural tool that allows the minority to force votes on the House floor if they collect a majority of signatures. The eastern Connecticut congressman also credited Jeffries with navigating government funding fights on top of not funding federal immigration agencies like ICE through regular appropriations.
“I think he really helped fashion the winning message, and I think the fact that there was no declared opponent kind of speaks volumes about the fact that people who know him up close really think he’s going to do good job,” Courtney said in an interview on his way into the House chamber to vote. “There definitely were some successful moments for a minority.”
For the remaining weeks of the session and in the new Congress, Jeffries will continue to work closely with U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, who is poised to take the gavel of the influential House Appropriations Committee.
Jeffries has pointed to DeLauro as one of the main negotiators working on government funding, which runs out after Dec. 11, and funding for the war in Iran. But by next year, DeLauro will be at the helm of the committee and will have a different negotiating posture.
Opposition efforts
A number of progressive and grassroots organizations in Connecticut have been rallying for alternatives to both Jeffries and Schumer.
Local groups such as Connecticut 50501 and Black Lives Matter 860 held a rally over the weekend in Hartford in the hopes of pressuring Connecticut’s lawmakers to vote differently. They want Blumenthal and U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, who is currently recovering from a stroke at a rehabilitation center, to support Van Hollen over Schumer. And they wanted House members to support U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., who was floated as a potential challenger but didn’t mount a formal bid.
“Both Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have proven time and time again through their votes that they stand for the establishment, for the billionaire class, for corporations, and not for us,” Alison Greenlaw, CT 50501’s Hartford County lead organizer, said in a statement. “Both accept significant contributions from AIPAC, which lobbies on behalf of foreign Israeli interests, not those of the American people. Neither supports Medicare for all. Neither supports abolishing ICE. Neither will vote to end the war in Iran. These are the clearly articulated priorities of the American people. If they do not support our priorities, they cannot set the agenda for the next two years.”
Greenlaw said groups like hers haven’t heard from Connecticut’s federal lawmakers in response to their push. She said they’ll be drafting a letter to political leaders and “exploring additional methods of applying pressure, based on their responsiveness, including future protests.”
Courtney said some of the calls to his office were “couched with caveats” acknowledging no one’s challenging Jeffries or from people saying they ultimately trust Courtney’s judgment during the final speaker vote in January. But the congressman said others were “definitely very fired up.”
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, said she also heard a lot of feedback from constituents and people around Connecticut.
“No one else is running. But also he’s done a good job, and he’s never led in the majority,” Hayes said in an interview outside of the Capitol on Tuesday afternoon. “I’ve got a lot of pushback, and I’ve tried to ask people, ‘Well, who would you suggest?’ And people either have no suggestions, or the names that they’re floating are people who are not even interested.”
“We have to be ready to lead on Jan. 3, so I don’t want us to be in a situation like the Republicans were with McCarthy,” Hayes said, referring to Republican Kevin McCarthy who struggled in multiple speaker votes in 2023 and was removed later that year.
Democrats are trying to look beyond leadership elections and give a sense of the agenda they’ll pursue next year with both majorities, though they’ll still need to contend with President Donald Trump’s veto authority over the next two years.
Jeffries has already outlined the early days of House Democrats’ majority. In a press conference a day before the internal elections, the congressman appeared to align with progressive U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ healthcare agenda with support for lowering the age for Medicare eligibility, including vision, hearing and dental care, and more. He said that’ll help “on our march toward universal health coverage.”
The New York Democrat said he also wants to end the war in Iran as well as Trump’s tariffs, restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, reverse Medicaid cuts enacted through the GOP’s major tax bill and implement campaign finance reform.
When the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, the full House will vote on speaker. Jeffries will need a simple majority.

Jeffries, a New York Democrat, will come into the 120th Congress with a comfortable majority following the midterm elections, and will aim to push through priorities, such as addressing skyrocketing healthcare costs and reining in an aggressive immigration crackdown and war in Iran, amid divided government.
“We know millions of people are drowning in this failed Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning things around,” Jeffries told reporters at a press conference following the vote.
“Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one: We hear you, we see you, we feel you and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you,” he added.
The Associated Press has called 257 House races for Democrats and 171 for Republicans, with seven races not yet called.
Democrats voted 251-11 to nominate Jeffries, lawmakers said while exiting the closed door meeting, where cheers could be heard. The support is well above the 218 votes he will need on the House floor in January to become speaker.
The House Democratic leadership also includes Rep. Ted Lieu of California as the Democratic Caucus chair, making him the first Asian American to hold that position.
Other members of leadership include Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as the Democratic majority leader, poised to become the first woman to take that role in the new Congress.
Pete Aguilar of California will be Democratic whip and Joe Neguse of Colorado will be assistant speaker. And Lauren Underwood of Illinois will be the next vice chair for the Democratic Caucus, which would make her the highest-ranking Black woman elected to leadership.
While Jeffries will have a Democratic Senate to work with, getting President Donald Trump to sign off on legislation that runs counter to his agenda will be a hurdle.
In the weeks since the midterm elections, Jeffries has laid out a handful of priorities for Democrats. At a press conference Tuesday, Jeffries said one of the early pieces of legislation he will bring to the floor is an immigration bill.
The measure, known as the American Dream and Promise Act, would provide a pathway to citizenship for people enrolled in Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, and to reissue legal protections for more than 1 million immigrants who were stripped of their Temporary Protected Status by the Trump administration.
House Republicans last week voted for Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan to lead them in the minority.

sources.text:
U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries has won the Democratic Party’s nomination to be the next Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives, paving the way for a historic election in January. Jeffries, 56, will make history as the first Black American to serve in the powerful role, which is second in the presidential line of succession.
Jeffries, who faced grassroots pushback against his nomination, earned an overwhelming majority of support from House Democrats, 251-11, in a closed-door meeting on Capitol Hill. The speaker will be officially elected after the incoming 120th Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
Despite the historic nature of his nomination, the longtime congressman from Brooklyn faced opposition to his candidacy for speaker. Some Democratic voters, particularly progressives, took issue with Jeffries’ policy stances on things like Medicare for All and U.S. military aid for Israel. Others felt his role as minority leader during the first two years of Trump’s second term was not sufficient when it came to resisting the Trump administration’s policies, including immigration, the war in Iran, and major funding cuts.
In a social media post, Jeffries reacted to the decisive vote with a picture of himself as a young child.
“Stay far from timid, only make moves when your heart’s in it, and live the phrase Sky’s the Limit,” wrote the incoming House Speaker.
Jeffries’ ascension came as a result of his tutelage under former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who handpicked him to succeed her after she stepped down as Democratic leader to usher in a new, younger generation of leadership.
“Congratulations, Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries!” wrote Pelosi in a post along with a picture of the two Democrats holding hands while seated across the aisle from each other on the House floor.
“This is a very surreal moment for me,” said longtime U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, who served in Pelosi’s leadership team for years and mentored Jeffries.
Ahead of Wednesday’s vote, Clyburn evoked the Black civil rights history of the moment, telling reporters, “When it comes to my turn to second this nomination, I’m going to be thinking about John, Lillian and Emily,” referring to the departed former U.S. Congressman and civil rights icon John Lewis, Lewis’ wife Lillian Miles Lewis, and his own wife, Emily Clyburn.
Jeffries has vowed to lead the Democratic Party in the next Congress to tackle the high cost of living by reversing what he and Democrats describe as the harms of President Donald Trump’s policies, including cuts to Medicaid and health care subsidies.
“Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one,” he said at a press conference on Tuesday. “We’re going to relentlessly fight for an affordable America. We’re going to work hard to drive down the high costs of groceries and gas and housing. We’re going to fight to make healthcare affordable for every single American and reverse the damage that’s been done.”
He added, “House Democrats are committed to ending this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran. We’re committed to stopping the Trump tariffs that have increased costs on everyday Americans by thousands of dollars per year, and we’re committed to getting big money out of politics.”

By Nolan D. McCaskill and Richard Cowan
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) – Democrats in the US House of Representatives will choose their nominee for speaker on Wednesday. For some progressive newcomers to Congress, it also marks the first opportunity to formally register their discontent with Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.
“We’re not going to rubber-stamp anything,” said Representative-elect Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, who has not committed to backing Jeffries. “We want to sit and have a conversation about the issues and what’s the plan going forward.”
Jeffries, a New Yorker who has led Democrats in the minority since 2023, is poised to easily win the closed-door, secret-ballot vote. A separate roll-call vote to elect the speaker of the House is expected on January 3, when Jeffries or incoming House Republican leader Jim Jordan of Ohio must clinch 218 votes to win the speaker’s gavel to lead the chamber and become second in line to the presidency.
While Jeffries is poised to be elected speaker in January, Wednesday’s vote will show how far he must go to unify a broad, diverse caucus that stretches from newly elected Democrats in President Donald Trump-won districts to insurgent democratic socialists ahead of that historic floor vote.
Under his leadership, House Democrats gained two seats in the 2024 election and have so far netted more than 40 seats in November’s midterm election, with several races still awaiting calls.
The internal vote will “give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned – based on track record, experience, vision – to help move us forward in the new Congress,” Jeffries said at a press conference on Tuesday.
PROGRESSIVE DISCONTENT SURFACES
The internal vote comes as progressive members, incoming freshmen and outside organizations have pushed for new Democratic leadership in the House and Senate. Protesters heckled Jeffries at Democrats’ “What’s Next” conference in Denver last week, and an apparent grassroots effort to draft progressive Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts into challenging him for speaker has gathered more than 150,000 signatures.
Pressley told constituents at a town hall in Boston on Monday that even though she holds the seat once held by former President John F. Kennedy and ex-Speaker Tip O’Neill, she doesn’t need the title of House speaker “to speak for the people.”
“I will always do that and continue to,” she said.
Jeffries has no challenger, and Democrats’ sweeping gains on election night took away the leverage a bloc of progressives could have held in a narrow incoming majority. Still, Jeffries has insisted he’s taking nothing for granted. He told reporters he would meet with leaders of three groups on Tuesday: the liberal Congressional Progressive Caucus, the moderate New Democrats and conservative Blue Dogs.
“We’re continuing to have conversations across the entire spectrum of the House Democratic Caucus family, talking to the new members,” Jeffries said. “They have a lot of wonderful ideas, fresh ideas, new ideas, about how to advance the ball in a bold way for the American people.”
FRESHMEN DEMAND POLICY FOCUS
Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine, a Jeffries supporter who has spoken to newly elected Democrats about the upcoming speaker vote, said many of them don’t know Jeffries and worry whether their voices will be heard on issues such as Israel funding, ending the Iran war and lowering healthcare costs.
“A lot of people who haven’t served in Congress before, it’s harder to see that role as herding cats,” Pingree told Reuters. “Sometimes people think that the speaker can tell us what to do. That rarely happens in Congress.”
Representative-elect William Lawrence, a progressive who flipped a battleground district in Michigan, told Reuters he has been saying since July he would back Jeffries and intends to keep his word.
“I have been hearing concerns from my constituents who want to know that this election will actually bring real changes, and so I do hope to hear a more ambitious agenda,” Lawrence said.
A group of incoming freshmen aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America told reporters last week that Democrats won by running on populist policies. Incoming freshmen Melat Kiros of Colorado and Claire Valdez of New York said their focus is on the agenda, not the individual leading it.
“What we’re demanding is an agenda,” Kiros said. “It’s about what kind of priorities, what kind of floor votes, what kind of plan do we have to actually fight for the bold change the American people sent us here to do.”
Jeffries has embraced some elements of progressives’ agenda, such as a federal minimum wage increase, a congressional stock trading ban, an overturning of the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision to get big money out of politics and an expansion of Medicare by lowering the eligibility age; adding vision, hearing and dental to coverage; and covering every child.
“Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage,” he said.
Forty percent of Democratic respondents have a favorable view of Jeffries in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, with 29% expressing an unfavorable view and 30% saying they haven’t heard of him or declining to take a position.
(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill. Editing by Michael Learmonth and Aurora Ellis)
