sources.news_title: Hakeem Jeffries speaker nomination: Democrats voting against
sources.text:
House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker on Wednesday by a 251-11 vote, putting him one step closer to becoming the first Black speaker of the House.
Jeffries secured the nomination without a formal challenger despite emerging resistance from some incoming progressives, who declined to commit their support ahead of the leadership vote. With no opponent ultimately stepping forward, Jeffries now moves on to the full House election in January, when the 120th Congress convenes.
"It is a high honor and distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as the Democratic nominee to be the next speaker of the United States House of Representatives," Jeffries said after the vote. "We know the American people are struggling in this failed Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning things around."
Read More on U.S.
Jeffries said his top priorities include lowering the cost of groceries, gas and housing, making healthcare more affordable and investigating the Trump administration, pledging that House Democrats would “hold the crooks accountable.”
Ahead of Wednesday's vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members. Yet having led the Democrats to one of the biggest incoming House majorities in decades, he has room to spare as he works to shore up support and tamp down dissent.
"The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic and transformational change," he said. "The status quo is unacceptable, and we are committed to delivering in a meaningful way the type of change that the American people deserve."
Democrats Voting Against Jeffries
Those opposing Jeffries, including some backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, signaled that talks are underway as they work to deliver Medicare for All, stop harsh Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions, get money out of politics and end Israel's war in Gaza.
Because the vote was conducted behind closed doors and by secret ballot, a full list of Democrats who voted against Jeffries was not immediately available. These are the lawmakers who have publicly said they voted against Jeffries:
- Claire Valdez, New York’s 7th District
- Darializa Avila Chevalier, New York’s 13th District
- Adam Hamawy, New Jersey’s 12th District
- Frederick Haynes, Texas’ 30th District
- Melat Kiros, Colorado’s 1st District
- Donavan McKinney, Michigan’s 13th District
- Chris Rabb, Pennsylvania’s 3rd District
- Don Leonard, Ohio’s 15th District
After Wednesday’s vote, seven of those representatives-elect—Avila Chevalier, Hamawy, Haynes, Kiros, McKinney, Rabb and Valdez—put out a joint statement explaining why they opposed Jeffries’ nomination.
“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," the statement said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”
Haynes, however, did not cast a ballot. A spokesperson said he “woke up unexpectedly ill” and tried to reach the caucus meeting in time but “narrowly missed the vote.”
“His intended vote was no, as per the released statement,” the spokesperson said in a statement share with Newsweek, adding that Haynes looks forward to working with his colleagues and Leader Jeffries on “Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, and ending the genocide in Gaza.”
Chevalier's office declined further comment when reached by Newsweek.
Leonard, who had previously said he would not back Jeffries unless he met a list of conditions, told Axios on Wednesday that he voted no.
What Democrats Have Said About Jeffries' Nomination
Most House Democrats backed Jeffries’ bid, and several celebrated the result on social media.
“Come January, Hakeem Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives,” Representative Frank Pallone of New Jersey posted on X. “His nomination today to be our Democratic candidate for Speaker is a watershed moment in our country’s history—and a perfect way to ring in this new Democratic majority that will fight for the American people. Congratulations, @RepJeffries!”
California Representative Mike Levin also posted on X: “This morning I cast my vote for Hakeem Jeffries to be our next Speaker of the House, and I was proud to stand with 250 of my colleagues as he won our caucus nomination overwhelmingly. Hakeem is a good friend and has been a steady hand through some of the most turbulent years this institution has seen. He kept our big, diverse caucus together, listened to every corner of it, and led us to our largest House majority in more than three decades.”
Two of the party’s longest-serving leaders, both leaving Congress in January, also weighed in. Outgoing California Representative Nancy Pelosi, who served as House speaker from 2007 to 2011 and again from 2019 to 2023, kept her congratulatory message short: “Congratulations, Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries!”
Maryland Representative Steny Hoyer, Pelosi’s longtime No. 2 and a former House majority leader, put the vote in historical terms. In a statement, he compared it to Thurgood Marshall joining the Supreme Court in 1967 and Barack Obama winning the White House in 2008, calling it “another historic step forward.”
Hoyer also framed the job as a test of governing. “The speakership belongs not to one party but to the Congress and to all Americans,” he said, adding that he had “great confidence” in Jeffries’ ability to deliver on “the affordability agenda the American people overwhelmingly voted for earlier this month.”
Not every Democrat was on board, though. Before the vote, Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey took aim at the holdouts.
“I stand by what I said: if winning in places we’ve never won before and having a historic majority isn’t good enough for a few of our members, then let them vote ‘no.’ But I’m team Hakeem,” he wrote on X on Tuesday.
Can Jeffries Keep Progressives and Moderates Together?
Much of the opposition to Jeffries’ speaker bid centers on his longstanding support for Israel and his ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), the pro-Israel lobbying group.
That dissent is unlikely to cost him the gavel. Democrats are poised to hold more than 250 House seats in the incoming Congress, giving the party an 80-plus-seat advantage over Republicans. That margin means Jeffries could withstand significant intraparty opposition and still reach the 218 votes needed to win.
But the pressure on Jeffries is unlikely to disappear after Wednesday’s vote. Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the progressive group Our Revolution, said Democrats will be judged on how they use their new majority.
“What we do with this majority will shape whether we can win in 2028 and beyond,” Geevarghese told Newsweek. “We won’t beat back fascism or repair the damage to our democracy by offering a milder version of the Republican agenda.”
He added that Democrats must show government can “raise people’s pay, make healthcare affordable, and hold powerful interests accountable,” arguing that doing so will require leaders to pursue changes even when the party’s own donors or leadership oppose them.
The demands started almost right away. Shortly after the vote, the Democratic Coalition called on Jeffries to subpoena the Epstein files and investigate Trump family business dealings and pardons issued by the administration.
Centrists see less of a split. Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at Third Way, a centrist think tank, said Jeffries will draw “overwhelming support from all three ideological caucuses.” He said the real task is keeping that support once the votes start.
“He also wants to remain Speaker so that means making sure the far left of the caucus doesn’t force litmus test votes that put Democratic centrist seats in jeopardy,” Kessler told Newsweek.
So far, Kessler argued, Jeffries’ health care promises to the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) stay inside that line. He said the top priority for most Democrats is restoring the Obamacare subsidies and reversing the Medicaid cuts in Trump’s reconciliation law. He called expanding Medicare to cover dental and vision care for seniors a longtime mainstream Democratic position. Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is a concession to progressives, he said, but “not a red line for the moderates.”
“So these commitments Jeffries is making to the CPC are the ones that moderate Democrats can swallow,” he said.
Kessler said the harder test comes later. He described this Congress as “a warmup test” for Jeffries, because the toughest work comes when Democrats also hold the White House and have to pass a president’s agenda.
“As we saw under Biden, that’s when the rubber meets the road,” he said.
New House Leadership: Who’s Who
House Democrats also elected party leaders on Wednesday. Unlike the speaker, the Democratic Caucus decides those positions internally, and they do not require a vote of the full House.
Democrats slated to assume those posts are:
- Majority leader: Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, currently the Democratic whip, was elected as the first woman in the position in an uncontested race. The majority leader is the No. 2 House Democrat, responsible for helping set the party’s legislative agenda and guiding legislation through the House.
- Majority whip: Representative Pete Aguilar of California, currently the Democratic caucus chair, was chosen to replace Clark in an uncontested race.
- Assistant speaker: Representative Joe Neguse of Colorado was selected in a unanimous vote.
- Democratic Caucus chair: Representative Ted Lieu of California was elected as caucus chair in an uncontested election. The Democratic Caucus chair, generally considered the No. 4 position in House Democratic leadership, leads caucus meetings and helps coordinate the party’s policy priorities, messaging and strategy. Lieu is the highest-ranking Asian American in U.S. House history.
As for the Senate, Democrats are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on December 1, with the vote taking place behind closed doors by secret ballot. Unlike Jeffries, who faced no formal challenger in the House, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is facing a direct challenge from Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who is campaigning for majority leader.
House and Senate Republicans have already held their leadership elections for the incoming Congress. House Republicans elected Ohio Representative Jim Jordan as minority leader, replacing outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson. In the Senate, Republicans reelected South Dakota's John Thune as their leader.
How Jeffries’ Vote Compares With Pelosi’s
Before Wednesday’s vote there was a lot of noise: a petition to replace Jeffries that topped 1 million signatures, approval numbers worse than Johnson’s and a bloc of incoming progressives who wouldn’t commit. Jeffries still walked out with about 96 percent of the caucus.
Pelosi did worse the last time Democrats flipped the House. She also ran unopposed in 2018. Of the 239 ballots cast, 203 Democrats voted for her, 32 voted against her and three left their ballots blank. She won roughly 85 percent.
On the House floor on January 3, 2019, she was elected with 220 votes, but 15 Democrats did not vote for her.
In both votes, most of the holdouts were moderates and freshmen pushing for a new generation of leaders, and many had promised voters in swing districts they would not back her.
Her other nominations went more smoothly. In November 2006, when she became the first woman nominated for speaker, Democrats picked her by acclamation. In 2020, the caucus met virtually and approved her by voice vote.
Jeffries had a unanimous vote of his own when he succeeded Pelosi as party leader in 2022.
What Happens Next
The 120th Congress is set to convene on January 3, 2027, when the House’s first major order of business will be electing a speaker. At that time, he will need 218 votes, a majority, to secure the gavel.
The grassroots campaign against him says it will be watching that vote. Nicole Whitted, who created an online petition urging Democrats not to support Jeffries, said the campaign, which has drawn more than 1.2 million signatures, wasn’t about any single lawmaker.
“It’s about whether the Speaker answers to the Democratic voters who just delivered this majority,” Whitted told Newsweek in a statement Wednesday. “On January 3, every member will vote on the record, and the more than 1.2 million people who signed this petition will be watching to see who members are listening to. Our voices deserve to be heard, and we’re not done using them.”

New leader of US Democrats pledges to target Trump corruption
Washington (United States) (AFP) – Hakeem Jeffries vowed Wednesday to "hold the crooks accountable" after Democrats nominated him to become the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives, setting the stage for two years of confrontation with President Donald Trump.
Issued on: Modified:
The 56-year-old New Yorker is poised to preside over a commanding Democratic majority following his party's sweeping midterm election victory, as his lawmakers prepare to reverse Republican policies and investigate the Trump administration.
Jeffries faced no declared challenger in the closed-door party election, but resistance from some newly elected progressives highlighted divisions over how Democrats should wield their newfound power.
"We're going to fight to make sure that, in the face of the unprecedented corruption, chaos, and cruelty visited upon the American people, that House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," Jeffries told reporters.
His warning came as Democrats unveiled plans for wide-ranging investigations into Trump officials and his business interests when they take control of the House in January.
Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, sent 12 letters Wednesday warning members of Trump's family and senior administration figures to preserve documents ahead of investigations into alleged corruption, immigration abuses and the handling of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
"This is just the beginning," Garcia said.
Historic milestone
Jeffries secured 251 votes in a secret ballot, with 11 cast against his nomination, according to US media.
He must still win a formal vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes on January 3, but the election is expected to be a formality given the Democrats' commanding majority.
He would become the first Black politician to occupy the powerful position, presiding over the House during the final two years of Trump's presidency.
Both returning Democrats and incoming lawmakers participated in Wednesday's ballot, with some progressives seeking concessions on issues ranging from US military support for Israel to the influence of money in politics.
Individual votes remained secret, with only the overall tally made public.
Ahead of the election, Jeffries met progressive lawmakers to discuss issues including Israel and healthcare, and he pledged Wednesday to tackle the cost-of-living crisis that helped propel Democrats to victory.
Brooklyn roots
"Our message to the American people, who are struggling in this failed economy, is a simple one: we hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," he said.
"We're going to fight for an affordable America."
Raised in Brooklyn's working-class Crown Heights neighborhood, Jeffries trained as a lawyer before entering the New York state legislature in 2007 and winning election to Congress in 2012.
Known for his measured manner, sharp rhetoric and penchant for quoting hip-hop artists, he became the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress when Democrats chose him to succeed Nancy Pelosi in 2022.
He also served as a House prosecutor during Trump's first impeachment trial in 2020.

Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past most skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker with the gavel.
Jeffries secured the nod during closed-door voting, 251-11, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January. Among those opposing him on the secret ballot were a group of progressive newcomers, who said in a statement there is “still work to be done” to ensure their priorities.
Afterward, Jeffries vowed to work hard, through every corner of the Democratic caucus, and said each generation has the opportunity to “show up, speak up, stand up, and help the country march toward a more perfect union.”
“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” he said, “and to get big things done for the American people.”
Jeffries, of New York, ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change in Congress after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media campaigns have been flooding the offices of Democrats in both the House and the Senate, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.
Andrew Coyne: America needs to make it easier to remove a president
Ahead of Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. Yet having led the Democrats to one of the biggest incoming House majorities in decades, he has room to manoeuvre.
Those opposing Jeffries, including some backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, signalled that conversations are ongoing as they push to deliver Medicare for All, stop harsh actions from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, get money out of politics and end Israel’s war in Gaza.
“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” they said in a joint statement.
Signing on as opposed were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York and Frederick Haynes of Texas, though he was one of two Democrats who did not vote. Reps-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres of California and Don Leonard of Ohio also said they voted against.
Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts – Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed and were elected, as was Rep. Ted Lieu of California, as chairman of the House Democratic caucus.
He will need a simple majority of 218 votes from the whole House to be elected speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. It would be a milestone in the nation’s struggles to create a representative democracy, since the first Black lawmaker was elected to the House more than 150 years ago.
U.S. Senate votes to advance sweeping energy legislation
Wednesday’s vote was the first of their careers for dozens of members-elect, before they’re even sworn into office in January.
Jeffries was nominated for House speaker by five Democrats essentially representing all aspects of the caucus, including Rep. James Clyburn, the legendary lawmaker from South Carolina.
“This is a historic moment for our nation,” Clyburn told the room, according to his private remarks that invoked voters’ outpouring for a change in the country.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro discounted the naysayers and said: “It is a day in the history of this nation that cannot be diminished in any way. I could never be more proud to be a Democrat than I am today.”
Rep. Kweisi Mfume of Maryland, who first came to Congress in 1987 with the late Civil Rights leader Rep. John Lewis of Georgia, said: “It just means so much in terms of moving the ball forward. Somebody’s got to break the glass, and in this instance that’s exactly what has happened.”
The tally, with 262 votes cast, included those elected to the new Congress and the House delegates.
Returning Rep. Emily Randall of Washington said earlier that she fielded questions about House leadership during town halls in her district and on her Instagram feed. So she decided to start dialling people back.
“People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the House,” she said, referring to the Vermont independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. “Technically yes, and it would be probably difficult.”
(It’s true that the House can elect anyone speaker, but it’s unlikely to be Sanders because he already has his day job in the Senate.)
She said she was voting for Jeffries. Lawmakers pointed to the livestream from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York trying to explain the role of the speaker and her support.
“There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries,” Ocasio-Cortez said earlier at the Capitol.
Five ways the midterm election results could reshape Donald Trump’s America
Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders after the Nancy Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.
When Pelosi, of California, stepped aside from leadership in 2022 after the party’s electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era.
A similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in elections next month.
Schumer insisted Wednesday he had the votes: “I will be re-elected as majority leader.”
Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House “are quite different.”
She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others. “His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction,” Ansari said.
Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who pulled off a stunning victory in a redrawn district favouring the Republican candidate, said before the vote that he’d be supporting Jeffries.
“It’s not even like a complex question,” he said about Jeffries, who he said “led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation.”
“I’m not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history,” he said.

Jeffries, 56, won the secret ballot vote 251-11, cementing his bid to be the first Black speaker in the House of Representatives. At least two members missed the vote: Representative Bennie Thompson, who was attending the Homeland Security Committee annual worldwide threats hearing, and Representative Lou Correa, who is out recovering from a medical procedure related to a recent heart attack.

Voters were also concerned about his perceived coziness to corporations and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. One Change.org petition for a new House speaker garnered more than one million signatures.
Jeffries and his team were able to aggressively fend off any challenges, and make support for the speaker appear practically unanimous. Even the House’s stalwart progressive, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, publicly supported Jeffries. There are certainly those who believe he was exactly the right person to take on a more progressive mandate.

President Donald Trump’s weaving waddle is raising red flags for health experts.

Trump’s $10 Billion BBC Lawsuit Is Massively Blowing Up in His Face
Donald Trump will soon be forced to explain himself.
Mandel NGAN/AFP/Getty Images
Donald Trump started a $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC, and now a federal judge has determined that he must formally participate to finish it.
U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz of the Southern District of Florida declared Tuesday that the president must sit for a deposition in January to advance the case, which centers on how the British Broadcasting Corporation edited the speech he delivered on January 6, 2021, for use in a documentary.
“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in a four-page order.
And Trump appears to be very willing, informing the court that he would be available for deposition between January 11 and January 22—a marked delay from the previous trial schedule, which gave Trump a deposition deadline of December 11. As a result of Trump’s proposed dates, the judge also revised the trial timeline, shifting the trial ready date from April 6 to May 3.
Trump sued the British broadcasting network for defamation, pinpointing the Panorama documentary “Trump: A Second Chance,” which spliced together comments that Trump originally made 35 minutes apart.
The BBC recognized and even apologized for this error but refused to pay him $1 billion for a tape that he claimed caused him “overwhelming financial and reputational harm.”
In a letter to the White House released last week, BBC chair Samir Shah said that both he and the entire network were “sorry for the edit of the president’s speech” and acknowledged that the editing choices created “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action.” At the same time, the letter laid out an abject refusal to take Trump’s legal threats further. “While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation claim,” the letter read.
But Kuntz did not agree, and last week decided against the BBC’s motion to dismiss by allowing Trump’s lawsuit to move forward.
“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” Kuntz wrote. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”
The DOJ’s Latest Legal Hires All Have the Same Red Flag
The department is lowering its standards for federal prosecutors.
Kevin Carter/Getty Images
The Department of Justice has been hiring an unprecedented number of deeply inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, a ProPublica report has found.
Looking at federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts, ProPublica found that over 50 young lawyers with fewer than three years of experience had been hired to the DOJ as assistant district attorneys, some with plans to become prosecutors. Of those 50, 20 had passed the bar exam within the last year.
“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school—it’s an astounding break with past practice,” Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney, told ProPublica. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.”
The second Trump administration has seen the largest departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in at least two decades, and the DOJ has seemingly been scrambling to replace the brain power that it’s lost—or at least the worker power. Elon Musk’s now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency offered employees money to leave their jobs, and by the end of January 2026, the DOJ had lost over 1,300 assistant U.S. attorneys, and replaced only about 470 of them.
By March, the department had hit its lowest numbers since 2014.
“If you are a lawyer, are interested in being an AUSA, and support President Trump and anti-crime agenda, DM me,” Chad Mizelle, who had just left his role as chief of staff at the DOJ months before, wrote on X in January, hinting that the DOJ was frantically searching for new hires.

sources.news_title: Jeffries wins speaker nomination despite far-left threats
sources.text:
Hakeem Jeffries is now all but certain to lead the House next January, a role that will make him the first Black speaker in US history as he oversees Democrats’ largest majority in years.
Roughly two weeks after their midterms romp, House Democrats voted to back Jeffries for the top job in the new Congress, despite some on the far-left clamoring for new leadership.
A small bloc of newly elected Democratic socialists had refused to publicly commit to Jeffries ahead of the leadership election, demanding concessions like votes for Medicare for All or a ban on arms sales to Israel.
But in the end, just 11 Democrats voted against him in the secret ballot vote, according to a source familiar with the vote, all but ensuring he will win the gavel in the new Congress.
“People of this country are demanding big, dramatic and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable. And we’re committed to delivering in a meaningful way the type of change that the American people deserve,” Jeffries told reporters after clinching the nomination.
A group of seven ultra-progressive new members declared in a statement that they voted “no” because they are still seeking commitment from Jeffries on key priorities, including votes on Medicare for All and ending “the genocide in Gaza,” they said. Signed onto the statement were Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.
Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard told CNN that he also voted against nominating Jeffries for speaker, emphasizing that he wants commitments that Jeffries will prioritize key issues like money in politics and blocking US aid to Israel.
“We’re looking for a strong commitment to end the Citizens United this Congress through a 28th Amendment, and we’re looking to call a vote on US aid to Israel,” said Leonard. “Until I get confirmation on those votes he does not have my support. We’ve got until the first week of January, I’m still holding out hope.”
Valdez later told CNN that she needed to “stand up” for the voters who elected her earlier this month: “I think there’s a lot that’s still on the table right now, and I’m really eager to continue conversations and fighting for everything we can at this moment.”
Asked about the defectors, Jeffries would say only: “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other.”
But other Democrats were more blunt about their frustrations. Rep. Hillary Scholten, a centrist from Michigan, complained that “infighting over leadership positions” would not help deliver on their campaign promises.
“There’s even still a few that you know didn’t want to own up to how they voted,” she said, calling out “a lot of disorganization in that segment of the caucus right now.”
Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who faced her own defectors during her leadership runs, downplayed the impact of those 11 Democratic “no” votes.
“I’m glad he took the vote so people could see how small the opposition was to him,” she said.“Don’t make a big deal. Each one of them is important. As 11, not so important compared to 250 some votes that he received,” she said.
Moments before he formally clinched the nomination, Jeffries received a powerful endorsement inside the room from Rep. Jim Clyburn, a longtime ally and one of the most senior members of the Congressional Black Caucus.
“Hakeem is interested in headways and not headlines,” Clyburn declared in his signature baritone voice, according to two people in the room, delivering a speech that one described as “powerful” as the caucus formally nominated the nation’s first Black speaker.
Now, all that stands between Jeffries and the gavel is a formal vote by the full chamber on the floor on January 3 — the first act of the new Congress — which his allies, and even his detractors, expect he will easily survive.
His leadership team will include Rep. Katherine Clark, who is set to become House majority leader – the first woman to hold that job – and Rep. Pete Aguilar, who will be the first Latino in history to hold the House’s No. 3 job of whip.
Democrats’ only competitive leadership election of the day – the vice chair position – also yielded a historic result. Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois will become the highest-ranking Black woman in Congress.
Inside the room, Underwood – who’s earned respect in the party for her heads-down approach to legislating – made a remark that was viewed by some fellow Democrats as a criticism of her competitor for the slot, Rep. Sara Jacobs.
“Being wealthy is not the primary or important qualification for leadership,” Underwood said in a speech just ahead of the vote, according to two people in the room.
Jeffries had always been expected to coast through the party vote on Wednesday, because the Democrats’ majority next year is simply too large for any small bloc of lawmakers to hold sway. But people close to the New York Democrat insist that he took nothing for granted.
Ahead of the election, he lined up face-to-face conversations with any incoming Democrats who had refused to commit — nearly all aligned with the Democratic Socialists for America. He sat down with the biggest factions of his caucus, including the centrists, New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dog Caucus, as well as the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
Jeffries and his team have kept their private discussions closely guarded. But Democrats have noted some subtle shifts in Jeffries’ public remarks, including a significant shift on one of the left’s biggest policy demands: Medicare for All.
Jeffries announced on Friday that he backs major tenets of a universal healthcare system, specifically, lowering the eligibility age for Medicare, creating a new program that guarantees universal coverage for kids and adding hearing, dental and vision coverage to the program.
It’s a major nod to progressive priorities, mirroring Sen. Bernie Sanders’ approach to a phase-in for Medicare for All system. (Centrist Democrats, meanwhile, have pushed for a Medicare-like public option.)

CNN’s Manu Raju and Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

Chris Van Hollen, a progressive, is challenging longtime party leader Chuck Schumer to be majority leader, no major contestant emerged against Jeffries in his bid for leadership — not even from the left wing of the party, where he has faced substantial criticism.
“He works with all different parts of the caucus,” Rep. Linda Sánchez, who chairs the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, told MS NOW on Wednesday. “We’re a big tent party. We don’t always agree, but we have more in common together with each other than we do with the failed policies of the Republican Congress and the Trump administration.”
Jeffries needed only a simple majority of his party’s support to secure the speakership, but he remained focused on his critics ahead of Wednesday’s vote. He met with progressive leaders Tuesday and requested his election be tallied on a recorded secret ballot, so critics could register their their opposition to his nomination.
His critics include several incoming House freshmen, at least six of whom — Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York — were among the 11 who voted against Jeffries’ nomination. Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes of Texas missed the vote due to illness, but indicated he would have noted against Jeffries as well; a statement released by the group initially said he had voted no.

sources.text:
House Democrats overwhelmingly backed Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) as their nominee for speaker on Wednesday, putting the New York Democrat on the cusp of becoming the first black speaker in U.S. history.
Jeffries won the Democratic caucus’s leadership election by a 251-11 vote, running unopposed in a secret-ballot contest that produced a recorded tally. The victory cemented his grip on the caucus after he helped lead Democrats to a commanding House majority in the midterm elections, securing at least 257 seats in the next Congress.
